::: {.chapter-lead}
The previous page, [GPT and Transformers: architecture and data flow](transformer.qmd), places self-attention within the network's forward pass. Here we isolate the three projections that feed it: **Q**, **K**, and **V**. These are not three token categories, but three learned transformations of a representation. Q and K determine the weights; V supplies the aggregated content. The next page derives the weights and aggregation themselves.
:::

<div class="epistemic-badges">
  <span class="epistemic-badge badge-concept">Verified concept</span>
  <span class="epistemic-badge badge-status">Architecture: Transformer</span>
</div>

::: {.callout-tip title="The essential idea"}
**Q and K determine the weights; V supplies the aggregated content.** This is the key distinction to retain before studying the attention computation.
:::

## Intuition: compare, then transmit

Imagine a collection of index cards:

- the **query Q** expresses what a position is looking for;
- the **key K** provides the vector against which that position can be compared;
- the **value V** carries the information that may be transmitted and aggregated.

The analogy separates the roles, but it is not a literal symbolic search: the model does not manipulate readable questions, labels, or cards. Q, K, and V are learned numerical vectors.

![Diagram of query, key, and value projections: Q and K determine attention weights, which are used to aggregate V.](../images/queries-keys-values-en.svg){fig-alt="An input representation is projected into a query, key, and value. Queries are compared with keys; the resulting weights are applied to values." width=100%}

## Where do Q, K, and V come from?

In self-attention, all three projections start from the same representation stream. For a sequence of $T$ positions, let this matrix be $X\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_{model}}$:

$$
Q=XW_Q,\qquad K=XW_K,\qquad V=XW_V.
$$

The matrices $W_Q$, $W_K$, and $W_V$ are learned jointly during training. They transform each input representation, but play distinct roles in the mechanism.

With $W_Q,W_K\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_k}$ and $W_V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times d_v}$, the resulting shapes are:

- $Q,K\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_k}$;
- $V\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_v}$.

The dimensions $d_k$ and $d_v$ therefore need not be equal. Optional biases are omitted here. To trace these projections in the actual block implementation, see the [guided Transformer-block walkthrough](transformer-block-walkthrough.qmd); general dimension and axis conventions are covered in the [tensor reference](tensors.qmd).

**Cross-attention:** this single-input formula describes self-attention, not every attention mechanism. In cross-attention, Q comes from the stream doing the querying, while K and V come from the stream being queried. See the [advanced cross-attention lesson](cross-attention.qmd).

## Keep these objects distinct

| Object | Role in the computation |
|---|---|
| Q and K | Determine comparison scores and then attention weights |
| V | Supplies the vectors combined using those weights |
| Attention weights | Determine each value's relative contribution to an output |

A key is not a human-readable semantic label, and attention is not nearest-neighbour search in the initial embedding space: scores are computed between learned projections. Likewise, the value closest to a query is not automatically the most useful: Q and K determine the weights, which are then applied to V vectors; values are not compared with one another to select the nearest one. The weights are neither the values nor a universal measure of semantic relevance. Their computation and interpretive limits are explained in [scaled dot-product attention](scaled-dot-product-attention.qmd).

::: {.self-check}
## Check the essential idea

[Extended exercises on Q/K/V and attention](exercises.qmd#attention).

**Which projections determine attention weights, and which one supplies the aggregated vectors? What happens if V changes while Q and K stay the same?**

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

Q and K determine the attention weights; V supplies the vectors whose content is aggregated. Changing Q or K can change the weights. If only V changes, the weights remain unchanged because the scores depend on Q and K; the aggregated content can change, but need not do so: weighted changes can cancel out.

</details>
:::
